title: Community and voluntary services on children and young people’s mental health
label: 27 October 2026 · Community mental health services for young people
summary: Representatives from charities and community organisations explained how they reach children and young people, described a steady rise in demand and complexity (especially anxiety and trauma), and argued services must be joined up, funded for the long term, and built around trusted non-clinical adults as well as clinicians. They welcomed policy shifts away from diagnosis-driven access, but warned that workforce shortages, short-term contracts and fragmented commissioning risk leaving the “missing middle” without help.

glossary.definition: Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services, the specialist NHS service for young people.
Mental Health Support Team based in schools, offering therapy, whole-school work and liaison with other services.
Integrated Care Boards, the local NHS bodies that plan and pay for health services.
Government-backed local hubs intended to give young people joined-up help for mental health and other needs.
Young people whose needs aren’t severe enough for specialist services but too complex for just universal support.
Young people Not in Education, Employment or Training.
Educational Mental Health Practitioner, a role delivering low-intensity treatments in schools.
A crisis-step-across service in Stockport offering help to young people who won’t reach the top of the CAMHS waiting list.

chapters.title: Who spoke and what they do
chapters.takeaway: Four charities described the services they run and confirmed rising demand, especially anxiety and trauma.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re hearing from community and voluntary organisations delivering children’s mental health support; please introduce yourselves briefly.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: I run TLC (Talk Listen Change). We focus on relationships and deliver counselling in schools, support for children affected by domestic abuse, whole-school work and a crisis service called Safe Zones in Stockport.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: I manage operations for Compass in Birmingham. We run 18 mental health support teams (MHSTs) there and about 45 across the country, working in schools and communities on therapy, whole-school approaches and liaison with specialist services.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: I lead the Well Centre. Our model trains youth workers as health specialists and embeds them into general practice and neighbourhood teams to reach the “missing middle” who fall between CAMHS and universal services.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: I run Northampton Saints Foundation. We use sports-based engagement to reach young people across education, employability and wellbeing—examples include our Engage programme for pupils on the edge of school exclusion or on CAMHS waiting lists.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Across our work we see rising demand and more complex needs: more anxiety, effects of social media, and trauma from domestic abuse; parents increasingly want diagnoses, but support should focus on needs now, not just labels.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: We’re seeing anxiety and emotional regulation issues but often alongside SEND, trauma and family problems. MHSTs aim to prevent escalation by building school capability, not just delivering one-to-one therapy.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: Our Lambeth evidence shows youth workers in health teams reach about 1,000 young people a year and can engage those who don’t fit clinic-based pathways, by meeting them in familiar places and supporting a broader set of needs.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Many children we meet are school avoiders or anxious about attending; sports-based programmes provide a trusted, non-clinical route back into learning and relationships.

chapters.title: Early access and prevention
chapters.takeaway: Early, school-based and community support works best when services meet young people where they are and support families too.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: How do you deliver early-access support so children get help when they need it?

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Whole-school partnerships work: assemblies, teacher training, on-site counselling and parent support. Safe Zones offers a step-across crisis option when CAMHS waits are years long—young people can re-refer when they need to.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: A simple front door, with good screening and triage, is essential. MHSTs do therapy, school-wide prevention and liaison. Often the earliest intervention is with parents or school staff, not always the child directly.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: Embedding youth workers in general practice creates a youth-friendly front door. GPs can hand off to a trusted youth worker who can hold the young person in the community, preventing unnecessary referrals to specialist services.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Early means different things. For us it’s reaching primary school children too, stopping issues escalating. Engage worked with children on CAMHS waiting lists and most who took part no longer needed CAMHS after our support.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Key point: stick with young people. Short courses won’t fit everyone; services must let young people re-access help when life triggers recur.

chapters.title: Joining up services and commissioning
chapters.takeaway: Providers want genuine partnership with commissioners and statutory bodies rather than short, competitive contracts.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What needs to change so local authorities, GPs and schools focus on early intervention rather than working in silos?

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: We need less silo-working and more collaboration around a trusted adult for the young person. Commissioners must design for partnership rather than hope it happens; otherwise organisations game KPIs instead of joining up.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Alliance contracts can work. In Greater Manchester we have a ten-year voluntary-sector alliance with the local authority that removed competitive bidding and encouraged shared goals and open-book discussions.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: Commission for integration: fund joined-up pathways and allow services flexibility to meet local needs rather than uniform contracts that ignore differences between schools and communities.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Short, year-to-year contracts make workforce and premises planning impossible. Longer funding horizons would help charities recruit and retain staff and build sustainable services.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: If the voluntary sector is treated as a co-partner in commissioning—on strategy and longer contracts—it reduces the risk of passing responsibility to financially fragile organisations.

chapters.title: Workforce: recruitment, training and retention
chapters.takeaway: Services need a funded national workforce strategy, training routes and stable pay to keep staff and expand coverage.

turns.speaker: Mark Sewards
turns.text: Are you having recruitment or retention problems?

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Yes—growing from a tiny team to around 50 has been hard. We recruit for values and train skills; lived experience often matters. Apprenticeships help, but suitable staff aren’t always available.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Pay and short contracts are the biggest issues. Charities can’t always match pensions or long-term security, so we lose people. Funding continuity is vital to retain skilled workers.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: MHST scale-up needs more than practitioners: leadership, supervision and career progression matter. Without a national workforce plan we’ll hit a quality bottleneck as coverage expands.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: We need training to create youth workers who can be health specialists—one foot in community, one foot in health. Over recent years many youth worker posts were lost; we must rebuild or retrain a workforce for integrated teams.

chapters.title: The 'missing middle' and transitions
chapters.takeaway: Young people between thresholds—and during transitions such as 16–18 or primary-to-secondary—fall through gaps unless pathways are joined and accountable.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: As CAMHS thresholds rise and waits lengthen, how have you adapted to the 'missing middle'?

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: We offer 'waiting well' support and step-across services like Safe Zones where five charities in Stockport provide help for those who won’t reach the top of a five-year CAMHS waiting list.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: Build capability in MHSTs and community teams, avoid making diagnosis the price of entry, and set up active navigation so families aren’t left to steer complex referrals alone.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: Fix transition gaps. Secondary-care cut-offs at 16 and adult services at 18 leave teens without ownership of their care; embedding support in general practice can bridge that.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: We target the missing middle through Engage, removing barriers so anxious pupils can spend a full school day with us and rebuild to mainstream education—many then no longer need CAMHS.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: Consider pathway-level accountability, not just organisational KPIs, so outcomes follow the child across services rather than measuring the number of 'bums on seats'.

chapters.title: Co-design, examples and digital tools
chapters.takeaway: Co-design with young people must be funded; several local examples show what works, and digital tools can help if used ethically.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: How do you co-design services with young people and what examples of good practice should we note?

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: We have a quality-and-engagement role in MHSTs to run pupil focus groups and school council work; pupil voice shapes what facilities or sessions matter to young people.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Being a small charity helps us adapt quickly to feedback—this year we added ASDAN qualifications because young people asked for them, and they now leave with recognised life skills.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: Co-design must be resourced. The voluntary sector does this well but it’s often unpaid extra work. Funded co-design means young people and lived-experience professionals genuinely shape services.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: Digital tools can help: we work with King’s College CAMHS Digital Lab on platforms for people on waiting lists. But if policies restrict some social media, we must ensure young people still have safe routes to support.

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: AI has a role in efficiency—freeing professionals for human relationships—if used ethically and in ways that protect the relational, human-centred work we do.

chapters.title: Policy asks and closing points
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged the Government to formally include the voluntary sector in strategy and commissioning, fund workforce development and prioritise prevention, and to tackle transitions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could pick two things for the Government’s mental health strategy for children and young people before Christmas, what would they be?

turns.speaker: Michelle Hill
turns.text: 1) Formally integrate the voluntary and community sector into strategy and commissioning. 2) Fund services that meet young people where they are, including non-clinical community settings.

turns.speaker: Arjan Bains
turns.text: 1) Sustained upstream investment in prevention and early intervention. 2) Scale what works locally but allow flexibility—model fidelity without forcing uniform delivery everywhere.

turns.speaker: John Poyton OBE
turns.text: 1) A workforce plan to train youth workers as health specialists embedded in primary care and neighbourhood teams. 2) Commission general practice to be youth-friendly so young people aren’t just passed on to long CAMHS waits.

turns.speaker: Jordan Letts
turns.text: Focus on transitions—identify where young people most commonly fall through and fund targeted support for 16-plus and other vulnerable transition points.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please write if you have anything further. This has been very helpful in understanding community services’ role and the system changes needed.
